title: Draupadi's sari

segments.voice: Yesterday: the dice, and a wise man who staked everything, one throw at a time. Your line was stop the hand. Did you put your hand down once? Day seventy-three.

Yesterday ended with the dice falling, and a woman lost in a game she wasn't even playing. Draupadi isn't in the hall. She's in the women's rooms. A servant comes to tell her she now belongs to the Kauravas and must come. And Draupadi, instead of coming, sends back a question. It's a sharp question, and nobody in that hall, not the kings, not the elders, can answer it. This is a hard scene. It's about a woman humiliated in public. We'll tell it carefully.
screen: `LOST IN A GAME SHE WASN'T PLAYING.` → `SHE SENDS BACK A QUESTION.` → `A HARD SCENE, TOLD CAREFULLY.`

segments.voice: Her question is this: when Yudhishthira staked me, had he already lost himself? Because if he had, he was a slave. And what right does a slave have to stake anyone? Duryodhana doesn't answer. He sends his brother Dushasana, who drags her into the hall by her hair. Standing before the whole court, Draupadi asks again, to everyone. The grandfather Bhishma, the elder everyone looks to, says the ways of dharma are subtle, and he can't say. Only one of the hundred Kaurava brothers, the young Vikarna, stands up and says she's right, and he's shouted down. Then comes the worst moment. Dushasana is ordered to strip her, in front of everyone. He grabs the end of her garment and pulls. And pulls. And the cloth keeps coming. Yard after yard after yard, a mountain of cloth piling up on the floor, until Dushasana collapses, exhausted, and Draupadi is still standing, still covered. In the popular telling, she has called on Krishna, and he answers her with cloth that never ends. Tellings differ on how much they say about how it happens, but in each of them the cloth doesn't end. Either way, the one who was supposed to be shamed is the one left standing. And the hall knows it. Bhima swears a terrible vow of revenge. Jackals howl, a bad omen. The blind king, frightened, finally offers Draupadi wishes, and she uses them to free her husbands. Her question was never answered. Her dignity was never removed. Unending.
screen: `HAD HE ALREADY LOST HIMSELF?` · `THE ELDERS CAN'T ANSWER.` · `THE CLOTH KEEPS COMING.` · `SHE'S THE ONE LEFT STANDING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your spine be straight, the way Draupadi stood. Think of a time someone tried to shame you: a teacher, a boss, a relative, a crowd online. Remember how it felt. Now notice something: you're still here. Whatever they took, they didn't get all of you. Let that be true for a minute. Then think of someone else who's being shamed right now, in your world or in the news, and picture them covered, protected, still standing. If you pray, you can hold them there. The bell holds the time.
Draupadi's sari. The cloth that wouldn't end, and a question the whole court couldn't answer.
Your line: unending. Today, if you see someone being shamed, even in a small way, be the Vikarna: the one who stands up and says it's wrong. Day seventy-three.

howItsDone: Draupadi's disrobing and the unending cloth are retold again and again in dance, theater and devotional song; devotees see in it Krishna's protection of those who call on him, and in parts of south India Draupadi herself is worshiped as a goddess.

original.note: Sanskrit: Draupadi, 'daughter of Drupada', the king of Panchala.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic sari.
what it means: a woman humiliated in public asks a question no one can answer, and the one meant to be shamed is left standing.
what a scholar hears: in the Pune critical edition the cloth still multiplies, but her call to Krishna is in the later manuscripts, not the main text.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Draupadi's question; Vikarna; the disrobing; Bhima's vow; Dhritarashtra's boons)

notes: Critical edition: the writer's understanding is that the Pune critical edition keeps the multiplying cloth but relegates Draupadi's explicit invocation of Krishna to the appendix. Please confirm before the trapdoor ships.
Karna's role (calling for her to be stripped) is left out for brevity; a Keeper may want it in.
Bhima's vow (to drink Dushasana's blood and break Duryodhana's thigh) is only called 'a terrible vow of revenge'; Draupadi's vow to leave her hair unbound is left for later.
Content care: the scene is a public sexual humiliation; told without graphic detail. Confirm tone.
